Lower the gradient window from injection 7 while preserving its slope and temperature to improve retention and test selectivity of the remaining close pair. The substantial time margin should allow better separation while keeping the last peak near or below 10 minutes.
Injection 9 already achieves the maximum CRF. Shorten tG by one grid step to test whether the run can be accelerated while preserving R ≥ 1.5 for the critical pair, currently at 1.62.

The steeper gradient improved the critical pair while retaining maximum CRF, so test a larger reduction in tG with the solvent window and temperature unchanged. This should shorten elution time and reveal whether another pair becomes limiting.

Continue shortening the gradient at fixed solvent endpoints and temperature, since the critical pair improved as tG decreased. Test 12 minutes to accelerate elution while checking whether the narrowing margins of other pairs still permit maximum CRF.

Shorten the gradient by one grid step while holding solvent endpoints and temperature fixed. The limiting resolution is now 1.91, so this tests faster elution with a reasonable margin above the full-credit threshold.

Test the next shorter gradient with all other settings unchanged to locate the fastest fully resolved method along this slope series. The pairs currently at R = 1.85 and 1.75 are approaching the threshold, so this step may establish the compression limit.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness by lowering phi1 one grid step, targeting recovery of the pair at R = 1.36. This intermediate slope should preserve faster elution than injection 13 while potentially restoring maximum CRF.

Raise temperature one grid step while preserving injection 15’s gradient to test a faster route beyond the slope-limited optimum. Monitor both close pairs for temperature-driven selectivity changes; injection 15 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Return to 25 C and lower the starting organic fraction to change selectivity of the limiting middle pair. Combine this with a steeper gradient to test whether improved initial separation permits faster elution while retaining maximum CRF.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention, paired with a shallower gradient to protect the compression-sensitive middle pair. Keep 25 C, since warming reduced its resolution substantially.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a substantially steeper gradient to see whether the limiting middle pair separates again after an elution-order crossover. At 30 C the later close pair had improved resolution, which may help tolerate this faster gradient.

Return to the maximum-CRF region and test an intermediate slope between injections 11 and 12 to improve the minimum-resolution margin. This prioritizes a more robust fully resolved method, since the faster exploratory conditions have sacrificed resolution and cannot improve the already maximal score.

Test whether a shallower gradient restores the middle-pair resolution lost at 30 C while retaining the temperature-driven improvement in the later pair. This may provide a faster fully resolved alternative to injection 20, with injection 15 retained as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction offsets the middle-pair selectivity loss at 30 C, while warming improves the late pair that limited injection 17. The slightly shallower slope than injection 17 should also help preserve resolution as temperature shortens retention.

Refine between the fully resolved 12- and 16-minute gradients at 25 C, where the two limiting pairs show opposing slope responses. This should balance their resolution margins near R = 2 while retaining maximum CRF and elution comfortably below 10 minutes.

Use a compact gradient with a slope close to injection 24’s balanced-resolution condition, but slightly steeper to shorten retention. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, preserving maximum CRF with approximately R = 2 margins for the limiting pairs.
